title: From Strategy to Subject to Classroom: The power of intellectual preparation and subject expertise
author: Lucy Gambier and Matt Howlett
summary: Lucy Gambier, Director of Secondary Education at Cornwall Education Learning Trust, and Matt Howlett, Head of Maths at Poltair School, preview their researchED Cornwall session on how a Trust's ambition becomes better teaching in tomorrow's lesson. They argue that shared language and shared resources are not enough without subject expertise, and that subject leaders are the people who connect Trust principles to the demands of a discipline. Howlett's example starts from a real problem: mini-whiteboards were in use but did not reliably show what each learner understood. They describe intellectual preparation as four connected areas: know the curriculum, know the learners, know the starting point, and bring pedagogical and subject knowledge together. Department meetings then pair preparation with rehearsal and end with a specific commitment about what a teacher will change in the next lesson. The authors are careful to say the approach still needs examination through classroom practice and evidence of learning.
points: Shared resources still require shared thinking, so teachers need to understand why a lesson sits where it does in the sequence and what it depends on.
A routine like mini-whiteboards only becomes purposeful when the question is chosen to reveal something specific and the teacher knows how to respond to the answers.
Intellectual preparation covers knowing the curriculum, the learners and the starting point, and combining pedagogical with subject knowledge.
Subject development meetings should pair preparation for an upcoming unit with rehearsal of a precise classroom practice.
Professional development has done its job when a teacher can say what they will change, when they will use it and what they will look for.
quotes: Teachers need to understand the thinking behind both: why a lesson sits here in the sequence, what earlier knowledge it depends on, what later learning it makes possible, and how its explanations, examples and questions support that learning.
These findings invite us to examine how improvement happens. They do not establish that a particular teaching framework or meeting structure caused those gains.
Mini-whiteboards were in use, but their presence did not always give teachers a dependable picture of each learner’s understanding. Some learners copied. Routines sometimes took too long.
The routine becomes purposeful when teachers know what learners’ answers reveal and how to act on them.
Think about your last department meeting. How much time did colleagues spend discussing the subject and how to teach it?
Professional development needs to reach the point where a teacher can say what they will change, when they will use it and what they will look for.
We need to look beyond whether learners have boards in their hands and consider whether their answers give teachers useful evidence, and whether teachers respond to it.
